what_its_for: Nalbuphine is a strong pain reliever (opioid) used to treat moderate to severe pain. It may be used before or after surgery, during labor and delivery, or for other types of serious pain that cannot be controlled with milder pain medicines.
how_to_take: Nalbuphine is given as an injection by a doctor, nurse, or other healthcare provider in a hospital, clinic, or medical setting. It is injected into a vein (IV), into a muscle, or under the skin. You will NOT give this medicine to yourself at home. Your healthcare team will decide the best way to give it to you based on your condition.
dosing: The dose your doctor chooses will depend on your weight, the type and severity of your pain, and your overall health. A typical adult dose is 10 mg every 3 to 6 hours as needed for pain. Your doctor may adjust your dose to find what works best for you. Never ask for more doses than prescribed, as this medicine can be habit-forming.
missed_dose: Because nalbuphine is given by a healthcare provider in a medical setting, you do not need to worry about missing a dose on your own. If you feel your pain is not being controlled or you think a dose was skipped, let your nurse or doctor know right away.
storage: Nalbuphine is stored and handled by your healthcare facility. If for any reason you have been given a supply to take home (which is rare), store it at room temperature between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep it away from light, heat, and moisture. Keep all medicines out of reach of children. Never share this medicine with anyone else.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while receiving nalbuphine, as this can cause dangerous drowsiness or breathing problems. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or making important decisions while this medicine is in your system, as it can cause dizziness and sleepiness. Tell your doctor about ALL other medicines you take, especially sleeping pills, anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, antidepressants, or any other opioid pain medicines, as these can interact dangerously with nalbuphine.
when_to_call_doctor: Tell your nurse or doctor immediately if you experience: slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme sleepiness or you cannot be woken up; severe dizziness or fainting; fast or irregular heartbeat; chest pain; severe nausea or vomiting; skin rash, hives, or swelling of the face, lips, or throat (signs of allergic reaction); confusion or agitation; or if your pain is not getting better. If you are at home and have a medical emergency, call 911 right away.
when_it_works: Nalbuphine usually starts working within 2 to 3 minutes when given into a vein, and within 15 minutes when given into a muscle or under the skin. Pain relief typically lasts about 3 to 6 hours. Everyone responds differently, so let your healthcare team know if your pain is not being controlled.
special_populations: Older adults (65 years and older): You may be more sensitive to the effects of nalbuphine, including dizziness and breathing problems. Your doctor will likely start with a lower dose and watch you closely. Pregnancy: Nalbuphine crosses the placenta and can affect a newborn baby's breathing if used close to delivery. It is sometimes used during labor under careful medical supervision. Breastfeeding: Nalbuphine passes into breast milk in small amounts. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding if you have received this medicine. Children: Nalbuphine can be used in children, but the dose will be carefully calculated based on the child's weight. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if your kidneys or liver are not working well. Always tell your doctor about all your health conditions before receiving this medicine.
